steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using LLMs to summarize U.S. court opinions for the general public. It should explain why accessible summaries of judicial opinions matter, what exists today, our GPT-4 summarization pipeline, the survey experiment we used to evaluate it, and end with a roadmap of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Judicial opinions, legitimacy, and the accessibility gap
2. Existing human-written summaries and their limits
3. LLMs as summarizers
4. Our pipeline
5. Survey experiment and findings
6. Evaluation protocol and the precision-accessibility trade-off
7. Paper outline

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Legitimacy and accessibility
- judges = important policymakers, less accountable to public than legislators
- legitimacy via written justifications based on shared principles, published as judicial opinions
- Rawls quote: [quote: Rawls on the Supreme Court as institutional exemplar of public reason]
- legitimizing function best served if general population understands
- in practice: extremely long, complicated technical language, only trained lawyers can read ("legalese")
- gap frustrates legitimizing function; may contribute to gaps in public trust in courts

2. Existing summaries
- SCOTUSblog, Oyez, Wikipedia summarize a few cases
- need highly trained legal experts -> costly; expensive and time-consuming even for lawyers
- only most high-profile cases summarized
- often still too sophisticated; lack procedural context, dissenting opinions

3. LLMs
- NLP/ML advances -> automatic summaries at scale
- LLMs such as GPT do many summarization tasks across domains
- generated summaries often preferred to human ones (prior work)
- legal contexts: GPT-4 passed the bar exam (prior work)

4. Pipeline
- GPT-4 extracts and summarizes facts of the case and principal arguments of majority opinion
- style targeted to contexts/audiences (social media, news articles)
- style transfer + simplification step -> accessible to non-technical audience

5. Survey experiment
- U.S. Supreme Court opinions; expert-written summary vs. AI-generated simple summary at seventh-grade level
- simple summary: better answers to basic factual questions
- higher qualitative ratings, more likely to share with friend or relative
- preferences even larger for respondents with low formal education

6. Protocol and trade-off
- combines evaluation of machine summaries with experimental social science practices
- trained legal professional read all summaries, satisfied with quality and faithfulness
- survey: do summaries make law accessible to non-experts
- novel: impact on target audience vs. metrics (word overlap, readability, fluency)
- precision-accessibility trade-off, not widely explored in NLP
- simplification trades precision for accessibility; survey: accessible summaries preferred and improve understanding

7. Outline
- Sec 2 related work, Sec 3 NLP pipeline, Sec 4 survey, Sec 5 results, Sec 6 discussion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Judges are important policymakers, but they are less accountable to the public than legislators are. Given this low accountability, one way judges strengthen the legitimacy of their policy choices is by giving written justifications based on shared principles, and these are published as judicial opinions. John Rawls argued that “[The U.S. Supreme Court’s] role is not merely defensive but to give due and continuing effect to public reason by serving as its institutional exemplar”. This legitimizing function is presumably best served when the general population can understand the written justifications. But in practice judicial opinions are usually extremely long and written in complicated technical language, which is inaccessible to anyone except trained lawyers. Because of this “legalese”, non-experts cannot read and comprehend the opinions. This gap in accessibility frustrates the legitimizing function of published judicial opinions, and it might contribute to gaps in public trust in the courts.

Since it is important to explain high-profile decisions to the public, there are several efforts to summarize court opinions for the public. SCOTUSblog, Oyez, and Wikipedia all provide summaries for a few cases. But such summaries can only be written by highly trained legal experts, so they are costly to produce. Even for trained lawyers, writing a summary is expensive and takes a lot of time. So only the most high-profile cases have summaries for the public. And even when summaries are available, they are often still too sophisticated for most readers. Also, the summaries often lack other important information, like the procedural context or the opinions of dissenting judges.

Recent advances in natural language processing and machine learning make it possible to generate these summaries automatically and at scale. Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT can automatically do many summarization tasks in many domains. Other work shows that these generated summaries are often preferred to human ones. LLMs have also been looked at in a number of legal contexts, for example another study shows how GPT-4 passed the bar exam.

We explore whether these models can effectively summarize court opinions. We present a pipeline that automatically generates high-quality summaries of court opinions. The pipeline uses GPT-4 to extract and summarize the facts of the case and the main arguments used in the majority opinion. We also show that the style of the summaries can be targeted to specific contexts and audiences, like social media or news articles. We combine this style transfer with a simplification step, and this makes the summaries more accessible to a non-technical audience.

We validate the accessibility and quality of the summaries with a survey experiment. For a set of U.S. Supreme Court opinions, participants read either an expert-written summary or an AI-generated simple summary written at the seventh-grade level. With the simple summary, respondents can better answer basic factual questions about the case. Respondents also give higher qualitative ratings to the simple summaries than to the expert-written summary, and they are more likely to share the summary with a friend or relative. For respondents with relatively low levels of formal education these preferences for the AI summaries are even larger.

Our procedure combines evaluating machine-generated summaries with established practices from experimental social sciences. A trained legal professional who is familiar enough with all summarized cases has read all generated summaries and is satisfied with their quality, especially their faithfulness to the arguments of the original opinion. Then we use a survey experiment to see whether the summaries help make the law more accessible to non-experts. This protocol is novel because it focuses on evaluating the impact of the summaries on a target audience, rather than assessing quality with metrics like word overlap, readability, or fluency that measure text quality in general.

Using a use-case-dependent and user-centric evaluation also shows another limitation of evaluating summaries based on quality: there is an inherent precision-accessibility trade-off, which has not been explored much in the natural language processing literature. Our simplification step gives up some precision in the summaries for more accessibility. The survey results confirm that our survey participants prefer the accessible summaries, and that the summaries also improve understanding of the opinions.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes related work. Section 3 describes how we developed an NLP pipeline for effective case summarization. Section 4 describes the survey experiment. Section 5 describes the main results, and Section 6 gives a concluding discussion.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Judges are important policymakers but are less accountable to the public than legislators. Given this low accountability, one way that judges strengthen the legitimacy of their policy choices is by providing written justifications based on shared principles, which are then published as judicial opinions. John Rawls argued that “[The U.S. Supreme Court’s] role is not merely defensive but to give due and continuing effect to public reason by serving as its institutional exemplar” [1]. Presumably, this legitimizing function is best served when the general population can understand the written justifications. In practice, however, judicial opinions tend to be extremely long and written in complicated technical language that is inaccessible except to trained lawyers. This use of “legalese” makes it impossible for non-experts to read and comprehend such opinions. The resulting accessibility gap frustrates the legitimizing function of published judicial opinions and may contribute to gaps in public trust in the courts.

Recognizing the importance of explaining high-profile decisions to the public, there are several efforts to summarize court opinions for public consumption. SCOTUSblog, Oyez, and Wikipedia all provide summaries for a few cases. However, only highly trained legal experts can write such summaries, which makes them costly to produce, and even for trained lawyers writing such a summary is expensive and time-consuming. Consequently, only the most high-profile cases have been summarized for the public. Moreover, even when such summaries are available, they are often still too sophisticated for most readers, and they often lack important additional information, such as the procedural context or the opinions of dissenting judges.

Recent advances in natural language processing and machine learning make it possible to automatically generate such summaries at scale. Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT [2] can automatically conduct many summarization tasks across many domains. [3] show that such generated summaries are often preferred to human equivalents. LLMs have also been scrutinized in a number of legal contexts; for example, [4] show how GPT-4 successfully passed the bar exam.

We explore these models’ potential to effectively summarize court opinions, and present a pipeline for automatically generating high-quality summaries of court opinions. The pipeline uses GPT-4 to extract and summarize the facts of the case and the principal arguments used in the majority opinion. We further show that the style of the summaries can be targeted for specific contexts and audiences, such as social media or news articles. We combine this style transfer with a simplification step, which makes the summaries more accessible to a non-technical audience.

We validate the accessibility and quality of our summaries with a survey experiment. For a set of U.S. Supreme Court opinions, we ask participants to read either an expert-written summary or an AI-generated simple summary written at the seventh-grade level. With access to the simple summary, respondents can better answer basic factual questions about the case. Respondents also give higher qualitative ratings to the simple summaries (compared to the expert-written summary) and are more likely to share the summary with a friend or relative. These preferences for the AI summaries are even larger for respondents with relatively low levels of formal education.

Our procedure combines evaluation of machine-generated summaries with established practices from experimental social sciences. A trained legal professional sufficiently familiar with all summarized cases has read all generated summaries and is satisfied with their quality, in particular their faithfulness to the original opinion’s arguments. We then use a survey experiment to investigate whether the summaries help make the law more accessible to non-experts. This novel protocol emphasizes evaluating the impact of such summaries on a target audience, instead of assessing quality using metrics such as word overlap, readability, or fluency [3] that measure text quality more generally.

A use-case-dependent and user-centric evaluation approach also highlights another limitation of quality-based evaluation of summaries: there is an inherent precision-accessibility trade-off that has not been widely explored in the natural language processing literature. Our simplification step trades lower precision in the summaries for more accessibility. The survey results confirm that our survey participants prefer the accessible summaries, which also improve understanding of the opinions.

This paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 describes related work. Section 3 describes the development of an NLP pipeline for effective case summarization. Section 4 describes the survey experiment. Section 5 describes the main results and Section 6 provides a concluding discussion.

References:
[1] Rawls (1993) John Rawls. 1993. Political Liberalism . Columbia University Press.
[2] OpenAI (2023) OpenAI. 2023. Gpt-4 technical report .
[3] Pu et al. (2023) Xiao Pu, Mingqi Gao, and Xiaojun Wan. 2023. Summarization is (almost) dead .
